questions.question: Which is the primary motivation for using matrix factorizations in machine learning models?
questions.choice_A: To ensure exact recovery of the original matrix under all conditions
questions.choice_B: To reduce parameters and computation while imposing useful inductive biases
questions.choice_C: To increase the dimensionality of the parameter space for better expressivity
questions.choice_D: To avoid any assumptions about the data-generating process

questions.question: For an m x n matrix approximated by a rank-r factorization W ≈ U V^T with U ∈ R^{m x r}, V ∈ R^{n x r}, what is the approximate parameter count (ignoring constants and biases)?
questions.choice_A: mn
questions.choice_C: r(m + n)

questions.question: Why is truncated SVD a common method for low-rank approximation in the Frobenius norm?
questions.choice_A: It provides the optimal rank-r approximation by the Eckart–Young–Mirsky theorem
questions.choice_B: It always preserves the largest singular values exactly while zeroing the rest
questions.choice_C: It minimizes the entrywise maximum absolute error
questions.choice_D: It guarantees improved generalization for any downstream task

questions.question: Which statement best describes the inductive-bias trade-off introduced by low-rank constraints?
questions.choice_A: Low-rank constraints eliminate overfitting without affecting approximation error
questions.choice_B: Low-rank constraints always harm expressivity and computation
questions.choice_C: Low-rank constraints increase variance but reduce bias
questions.choice_D: Low-rank constraints reduce hypothesis space, potentially improving generalization but limiting expressivity

questions.question: What is a typical computational advantage of block-diagonal matrices in neural networks?
questions.choice_A: They guarantee orthogonality of the overall transform
questions.choice_B: They enable independent, parallel computation on smaller subspaces
questions.choice_C: They minimize the spectral norm of the transform
questions.choice_D: They ensure full connectivity across all features

questions.question: What distinguishes a block-sparse matrix from a general sparse matrix in the context of structure?
questions.choice_A: Block-sparse matrices always have fewer nonzeros than general sparse matrices
questions.choice_B: Block-sparse matrices cannot be used in neural networks
questions.choice_C: General sparse matrices encode convolutional structure
questions.choice_D: Block-sparse matrices restrict nonzeros to structured sub-blocks, enabling hardware-friendly patterns

questions.question: Which property is true of permutation matrices P?
questions.choice_A: P is orthogonal, and P^{-1} = P^T
questions.choice_B: P has nonzero entries only on the diagonal
questions.choice_C: P diagonalizes every symmetric matrix
questions.choice_D: P is positive definite

questions.question: What is the computational cost of multiplying a diagonal matrix D ∈ R^{n x n} by a vector x ∈ R^n, and why?
questions.choice_A: O(n^2), because each output depends on all inputs
questions.choice_B: O(1), because diagonal matrices are constant-time operations
questions.choice_C: O(n), because each output is a single elementwise product
questions.choice_D: O(n log n), due to fast transforms

questions.question: Suppose W ∈ R^{(p r) x (q s)} is represented as a Kronecker product W = A ⊗ B with A ∈ R^{p x q} and B ∈ R^{r x s}. How many parameters does this representation use, ignoring biases?
questions.choice_A: p r + q s
questions.choice_B: p q + r s
questions.choice_C: p q r s
questions.choice_D: (p + q)(r + s)

questions.question: Which statement about the rank of a Kronecker product is correct?
questions.choice_A: rank(A ⊗ B) = max(rank(A), rank(B))
questions.choice_B: rank(A ⊗ B) = rank(A) + rank(B)
questions.choice_C: rank(A ⊗ B) = min(rank(A), rank(B))
questions.choice_D: rank(A ⊗ B) = rank(A) · rank(B)

questions.question: Why are circulant matrices attractive for fast linear transforms in machine learning?
questions.choice_A: They are diagonalized by the discrete Fourier transform, enabling O(n log n) multiplications via FFT
questions.choice_B: They guarantee better approximation error than SVD truncation
questions.choice_C: They require no parameters to store
questions.choice_D: They are always low-rank

questions.question: Which statement correctly characterizes Toeplitz matrices in terms of structure and algorithms?
questions.choice_A: Toeplitz matrices are diagonal in the Fourier basis
questions.choice_B: Toeplitz matrices have rank-1 plus diagonal structure
questions.choice_C: Toeplitz matrices have low displacement rank, enabling fast structured algorithms
questions.choice_D: Toeplitz matrices cannot be used to express convolutions

questions.question: How does parameter sharing in convolutions relate to structured matrices?
questions.choice_A: It induces dense random matrices with no structure
questions.choice_B: It corresponds to Toeplitz (1D) or block-Toeplitz with Toeplitz blocks (2D) matrices with tied parameters
questions.choice_C: It produces orthogonal matrices by construction
questions.choice_D: It enforces low rank in the frequency domain

questions.question: What is a common trade-off when imposing strong structure (e.g., low-rank, Toeplitz, Kronecker) on weight matrices?
questions.choice_A: Guaranteed reduction in approximation error for any dataset
questions.choice_B: No change in parameter count but faster training
questions.choice_C: Increased parameter count but improved generalization
questions.choice_D: Reduced parameter count and computation at the risk of underfitting or missed patterns

questions.question: Which transformation shows a basic non-uniqueness in Kronecker factorizations W = A ⊗ B?
questions.choice_A: Replace A with cA and B with (1/c)B for any nonzero scalar c
questions.choice_B: Replace A with A + B and B with A − B
questions.choice_C: Replace A with A^T and B with B^T
questions.choice_D: Replace A with A^2 and keep B unchanged

questions.question: Which regularization is a convex surrogate that encourages low-rank solutions when directly minimizing rank is intractable?
questions.choice_A: Entrywise L2 regularization
questions.choice_B: Spectral norm penalty squared
questions.choice_C: Nuclear norm (sum of singular values)
questions.choice_D: Entrywise L0 penalty

questions.question: What is an advantage of block-diagonal layers for modular architectures such as mixture-of-experts?
questions.choice_A: They guarantee equal utilization of all experts
questions.choice_B: They ensure universal function approximation with fewer parameters
questions.choice_C: They make routing unnecessary
questions.choice_D: They reduce cross-talk across experts, allowing specialization within blocks

questions.question: Given a factorized weight matrix W = U V^T with U ∈ R^{m x r}, V ∈ R^{n x r}, what is the typical cost to multiply W by a vector x ∈ R^n using the factors, and why?
questions.choice_A: O((m + n) r), by computing t = V^T x then U t
questions.choice_B: O(m n), because the product is dense
questions.choice_C: O(r^2), due to the r-dimensional bottleneck
questions.choice_D: O(n log n), by using FFT

questions.question: In graph-structured models, why does permutation similarity A' = P^T A P matter?
questions.choice_A: It randomizes the spectrum of A
questions.choice_B: It reindexes nodes without changing eigenvalues, reflecting permutation equivariance
questions.choice_C: It converts A to a diagonal matrix
questions.choice_D: It ensures A' has lower rank

questions.question: When selecting between low-rank and sparsity constraints for compression, which rule-of-thumb is most appropriate?
questions.choice_A: Prefer sparsity when features are globally correlated and low-rank when connections are isolated
questions.choice_B: Prefer low-rank only when the matrix is diagonal
questions.choice_C: Prefer low-rank when correlations are global and redundant; prefer sparsity when only a few connections are salient
questions.choice_D: Always prefer low-rank because it reduces parameters the most
